scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9103: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports they have completely
lost connectivity to the partner network -- they cannot reach pc2 (200.1.1.2) in
the peer AS since this morning. The team is convinced someone fat-fingered the
BGP configuration overnight and want the BGP config rolled back. Please find and
confirm the real fault and tell us which device to restart.

injection.action: administratively down the inter-AS interface (eth0) on router1

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth0 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is the inter-AS link: router1's eth0 (the interface to router2)
is DOWN, so the physical/L2 path between the two ASes is broken. As a CONSEQUENCE
the eBGP session between router1 and router2 drops and the inter-AS prefixes are
withdrawn, so pc1 (195.11.14.2) cannot reach pc2 (200.1.1.2). The ticket
MISDESCRIBES the cause as a BGP configuration error, but the BGP configuration is
intact and unchanged -- the session is down purely because the underlying link is
down, not because of any config mistake.

The correct diagnosis identifies router1 (inter-AS link / eth0 down) as the root
cause and explicitly notes the BGP loss is a downstream EFFECT, not the cause: the
BGP configuration on router1 and router2 is unchanged, so the user's "someone
broke the BGP config" hypothesis is wrong. An agent that rolls back / blames the
BGP configuration has accepted the ticket's misdescription instead of testing it.
scenario.fix_spec:
Bring the inter-AS link back up: on router1 run `ip link set eth0 up`. Once eth0
is up again, the eBGP session to router2 re-establishes, the inter-AS prefixes are
re-exchanged, and pc1 reaches pc2 normally. The BGP configuration needs no change
-- it was never modified.
scoring_axes: must-identify-link-down: identifies the inter-AS link (router1 eth0) is down as the root cause, with BGP loss as a consequence
bonus-rules-out-bgp-config: notes the BGP configuration is intact/unchanged, rejecting the "misconfigured BGP" cause

line.command: ip -br link show eth0 | grep -c UP

agent.diagnosis_text:
The affected component is the inter-router peering link on router1 (interface eth0) carrying the eBGP session to router2. Mechanism: pc1’s traffic to 200.1.1.0/24 is sent to router1, but router1 has no route to that network because its eBGP session to router2 is not established. Consequently, router1 immediately returns “Destination Net Unreachable,” matching the user symptom.

Localization: On router1, eth0 (toward router2) is down at L2/L3:
- ip link show dev eth0: state DOWN; ethtool: Link detected: no.
- FRR on router1 shows the BGP neighbor 193.10.11.2 stuck in Active (no session), and router1’s routing table contains only the directly connected 195.11.14.0/24 (no 200.1.1.0/24).
On router2, the peering interface eth0 is UP (ethtool: Link detected: yes), but it cannot ping 193.10.11.1 and will age out the session; its current “Established” state reflects stale TCP until hold-time expiry.

Root cause: router1’s peering interface eth0 is administratively/physically down, breaking the eBGP session and removing reachability to 200.1.1.0/24.

Corrective fix: Restore the inter-router link on router1. Either:
- Bring the interface up: on router1, run “ip link set eth0 up”, or
- Restart the device (as requested): restart router1 to reinitialize its NICs, then verify “show ip bgp summary” forms Established and that routes to 200.1.1.0/24 appear. No BGP configuration rollback is required.

per_axis.rationale: Clearly states router1's eth0 inter‑AS link is down as the root cause and that the BGP session loss is a consequence (recommends restoring the interface).

per_axis.axis: bonus-rules-out-bgp-config: notes the BGP configuration is intact/unchanged, rejecting the "misconfigured BGP" cause
per_axis.rationale: The diagnosis attributes failure to router1's eth0 being down and explicitly states no BGP configuration rollback is required, rejecting a misconfigured BGP cause.
Recommends bringing router1's eth0 back up (ip link set eth0 up) or restarting the router, which restores the inter-AS link and allows the eBGP session and routes to return.

The investigation log shows router1's eth0 is DOWN, pc1's pings get 'Destination Net Unreachable' from router1, and router2's interface is UP with a BGP neighbor still showing Established — supporting the conclusion that the physical link on router1 is the root cause and BGP loss is an effect.
